t: Maximize Palindrome Length From Subsequences - Interval DP Across Two Strings
o: We pick a non-empty subsequence from each word and concatenate them; the target is the longest possible palindrome. Because subsequence1 precedes subsequence2 by construction, any qualifying palindrome begins with a character taken from word1 and ends with one taken from word2 - its outermost pair straddles the boundary and consists of equal characters. In Example 1, pinning word1's 'a' (index 1) against word2's final 'a' leaves "cbcbb" in between, whose longest palindromic subsequence is "cbc" (3), totaling 5 = "abcba". Example 2 pairs 'a'(word1[0]) ... 'a'(word2[1]) with 'b' inside, giving "aba" of length 3. Example 3 has no equal boundary-spanning pair at all, hence 0. Concatenating the words and running the classic interval DP for longest palindromic subsequence - restricted to endpoints from different words - solves it within O(n^2) for lengths up to 1000 each.
k: Both subsequences must be non-empty, so a valid palindrome's endpoints come from different words: word1[i] ... word2[j] with s[i] == s[j].
Fix such an outer pair and the interior decouples: candidate = 2 + LPS(concat, i+1, j-1), maximized over boundary-spanning pairs.
This is the standard LPS interval dp on word1 + word2 plus one restriction - never report a palindrome living wholly inside a single word.

a.i: Define lps(i, j) as the longest palindromic subsequence inside concat[i..j] with the three familiar cases (empty span, single character, equal ends, otherwise skip one end) and memoize it. Then try every candidate outer pair - i inside word1, j inside word2, equal characters - and maximize 2 + lps(i+1, j-1). The recursion falls straight out of the palindrome definition, which makes it the easiest version to reproduce under pressure, and lazy evaluation touches only the cells actually needed.
s: Let s = word1 + word2 and define a memoized lps(i, j).
Cases: i > j -> 0; i == j -> 1; s[i] == s[j] -> lps(i+1, j-1) + 2; else max(lps(i+1, j), lps(i, j-1)).
For every i < len(word1) <= j with s[i] == s[j], consider 2 + lps(i+1, j-1).
a.t: O((n+m)^2) time - each interval is solved once in O(1) after memoization; the outer double loop visits O(n*m) boundary pairs.
a.sp: O((n+m)^2) space for the memo table, plus recursion depth up to n+m (raise Python's limit accordingly).

a.i: Fill the identical dp table iteratively over increasing interval length and fold the global best directly into the transition: whenever s[i] == s[j] and the endpoints satisfy i < len(word1) <= j, dp[i][j] is a legal full-palindrome length. One condition enforces the non-empty-both-sides rule without a separate pass. Bottom-up avoids recursion-depth pitfalls and carries smaller constants, at the cost of computing every cell even when few boundary pairs exist.
s: Set s = word1 + word2; allocate dp where dp[i][j] stores the LPS of s[i..j].
Equal ends: dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2 (reads 0 harmlessly when j = i+1); else max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
Whenever s[i] == s[j] and i < len(word1) <= j, update the answer with dp[i][j].
a.t: O((n+m)^2) time - every interval of the concatenation is filled exactly once with O(1) transitions.
a.sp: O((n+m)^2) space for the table (reducible to O(n) rolling rows since only row i+1 is ever read).

w: Deliver bottom-up: no recursion limits, predictable memory, easy extension. The classic bug is returning the unconstrained LPS of the concatenation - for `word1 = "aa"`, `word2 = "bb"` that yields 2 ("aa"), but the correct answer is 0 because no boundary-spanning pair matches; the non-empty constraint lives entirely in that endpoint check. Also note dp[i+1][j-1] when the outer pair is adjacent reads a below-diagonal zero and correctly yields 2. Follow-ups: reconstruct the palindrome itself (parent pointers or recomputation), allow empty subsequences (collapses to plain LPS of the concatenation), or extend to three words with two boundaries.
